Yes—at least some materials-science workflows suggest you can use an LLM to propose experiments without training a model. For example, Wang et al. propose an LLM-based active learning framework (LLM-AL) that leverages pretrained knowledge to propose experiments from text-based descriptions, operating in an iterative few-shot setting rather than training a new model on the materials task. [1]

Related approaches embed LLMs inside optimization/search loops to guide which experiments to run next, also avoiding training task-specific predictive models. Chen et al. (LABO) uses LLM predictions and a gating criterion within a Bayesian optimization loop to decide when to rely on LLM evaluation versus costly experiments. [6] Guo’s LacMaterial uses analogical reasoning to generate novel battery materials candidates beyond conventional substitutions via prompt-based strategies. [2]

These papers differ in emphasis: [1] is specifically an “active learning” experiment-selection framework; [6] focuses on sample-efficient Bayesian optimization with LLM evaluations; [2] focuses on analogical hypothesis generation for materials candidates rather than explicit experimental active learning.
